plain: Anything the office values and must protect: data, systems, devices, people's trust.
Something or someone that could cause harm: an attacker, a flood, a careless click.
A weakness a threat can use: an old system, a shared password, a missing step.
How probable it is that the harm happens.
How bad it is if the harm happens.
Likelihood × impact: how much a possible harm should worry us.
Anything that lowers a risk: a rule, a habit, a lock, a setting.
Malicious software that locks files and demands payment to unlock them.
Threatening to leak or destroy data unless the victim pays.
An attacker who acts for a political or social cause rather than money.
A fake message that tricks you into clicking, paying or giving away a password.
Multi-factor login: a password plus a second proof, such as a code on your phone.
An update that fixes a known weakness in software.
When a maker stops fixing a product. Its weaknesses stay open for good.
Any information that identifies a person, alone or with other details (RA 10173 Sec. 3(g)).
Personal information that can cause greater harm: health, age, religion, marital status, government ID numbers and more (Sec. 3(l)).
The person the data is about.
The organization that decides why and how personal data is used.
An organization that handles personal data only on the controller's instructions.
The person who makes sure the office follows the Data Privacy Act.
Personal data seen, changed, lost or destroyed when it should not be.
Enough facts that a sensible person would think a breach happened. You do not need proof.
The NPC's online Data Breach Notification Management System.
The National Privacy Commission, which enforces the Data Privacy Act.
Scrambling data so only someone with the key can read it.
Information security management system: the ongoing way an office plans, runs, checks and improves its security.
The list of Annex A controls an office uses, and why it uses or skips each one.
AI that writes text, pictures, audio or video on request.
A fake video, picture or voice made with AI to look real.
Signed information attached to a file that shows where it came from and how it was edited.
A network with no internal walls, so one infected computer can reach all the others.
A 0 to 10 score for how severe a software weakness is.
Six kinds of threat: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege.
A line on a data flow map where data passes between areas with different levels of trust.
Tricking people, rather than computers, into giving access or money.
An email setting that tells other servers what to do with mail that fakes your office's address.
A phishing message written for one person, using details about them.
Phishing by text message (SMS).
Phishing by phone call (voice).
Phishing through a QR code that leads to a fake site.
Inventing a believable story to get information or help.
Leaving something tempting, like a USB stick, so someone plugs it in.
Following an authorized person through a locked door.
A fake or hijacked email from a boss or supplier asking for a payment.
Sending login prompts again and again until someone taps Yes.
Seven steps most attacks go through, from scouting to stealing. Breaking any step stops the attack.
A site's digital ID, issued by a certificate authority, that lets your browser check it is talking to the right site.
A mark made with a private key that proves who sent a file and that it was not changed.
The public zone: the part of a network that holds public services, kept apart from internal systems.
Sign-in methods based on a key held on your device, which a fake site cannot use.
A gatekeeper that allows or blocks connections according to rules.
Turning data into a fixed fingerprint; any change gives a different fingerprint.
Systems that detect suspicious activity and alert (IDS), or also block it (IPS).
The person responsible for keeping, and recovering, an encryption key.
Giving only the access a job needs, only for as long as it is needed.
Role-based access control: access given to roles that match job functions.
Dividing a network into zones that each reach only what they need.
Splitting a task so no one person can complete a risky action alone. Also called segregation of duties.
The protection behind HTTPS that encrypts data moving between a browser and a site.
An encrypted tunnel between a remote computer and the office network.
A web application firewall, which inspects requests sent to a website.
A strategy of checking every request, assuming breach, and granting least privilege.
A regular check that every account still needs the access it has.
A browser page saying it cannot confirm the site's identity.
Approving, recording and testing a change before it is made.
Tools that warn or block when sensitive data leaves by email, upload or USB.
Hiding part of a value, such as showing only the last four digits of an ID number.
An account nobody has used for a long time.
Any device that connects to office systems: laptop, desktop, phone or tablet.
Software that detects and blocks malware on a device.
Encryption of everything stored on a device, so a lost device does not expose its data.
One login used by several people, so no one is accountable for what it does.
CISA's list of weaknesses that attackers are known to be using.
A web address made to resemble a real one.
Mobile device management controls a whole device; mobile app management protects only the work apps.
An account that can change settings or other people's access.
The share of staff who report a suspicious message.
Apps, sites, accounts or devices used for office work without approval.
A daily account without administrator rights.
Information about threats, analysed so that an office can act on it.
Traffic Light Protocol: labels that say how far a report may be shared.
Blocking known malicious or unwanted websites.
